what_it_does: When a chip pattern is printed onto a silicon wafer using light (a process called lithography), a chemical step called post-exposure bake (PEB) causes acids to spread and react inside the light-sensitive coating, shaping the final circuit pattern. Simulating this diffusion precisely in 3D is slow but critical for predicting whether the printed pattern will come out correctly. This paper applies a neural-network model called Mamba — a newer architecture designed for efficiently processing long sequences of data — to predict the 3D result of PEB faster than traditional physics solvers. The network uses a hierarchical design that captures both coarse structure and fine details at multiple scales, and the Mamba component scans the 3D volume in a structured way to model how the acid spreads in all directions. This is a machine-learning shortcut that approximates an expensive simulation, which is valuable during chip design when engineers need to run thousands of such simulations to optimize patterns.
